title: Substantial disagreement between satellite- and ground-level nighttime light patterns revealed by SDGSAT-1 and street view imagery
abstract: Over the past three decades, nighttime light (NTL) has become one of the most widely used and powerful proxies for characterizing human activities. Despite the recent proliferation of available NTL data from both satellite- and ground-level sensors, intrinsic differences between these two observation approaches can result in distinct NTL brightness patterns (satellite-ground disagreement). Such disagreement, particularly its spatial heterogeneity, represents a critical yet largely overlooked issue in NTL studies, introducing uncertainty into the interpretation and application of NTL observations. Here, by incorporating SDGSAT-1 glimmer imagery and panoramic nighttime street view imagery with geospatial AI approaches, we present a spatially explicit, wall-to-wall investigation into satellite-ground disagreement across Singapore. Specifically, we characterized citywide disagreement and its variation across land-use types, analyzed contributing factors, and assessed its implications for NTL-based applications, reinforced by Monte Carlo-based uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analyses using independent observations from Singapore and Shenzhen, China. Our study revealed substantial and spatially heterogeneous satellite-ground disagreement across Singapore. Relative disagreement averaged 15% ± 13% citywide but reached 42% ± 12% in 13% of the city. Such pronounced heterogeneity was likewise evident across land-use types, with commercial areas standing out for consistently significant disagreement, where ground-level NTL brightness was 29% ± 26% higher than satellite-level NTL brightness. Building morphology, vegetation canopy cover, and sensor spectral response contributed to satellite-ground disagreement, suggestive of distinct mechanisms underlying the identified patterns. Applying satellite- and ground-level NTL data yielded relative differences of at least 115% and 83% in GDP estimation and NTL exposure inequality assessment, respectively. This study sheds new light on satellite-ground disagreement by moving beyond discrete comparisons toward a comprehensive analysis of its heterogeneity and implications, thereby establishing an empirical basis for integrating NTL observations and contributing to more reliable NTL-based applications and evidence-informed policies on sustainable urbanization.

title: Evaluating multi-satellite VIIRS active fire observations as a burned area proxy across North America
Divergent transpiration regulation among 20 urban tree species under extreme heat revealed by UAV multisource remote sensing
abstract: Urban areas face increasing extreme heat risk, yet satellite remote sensing struggles to quantify crown-scale transpiration in heterogeneous urban landscapes. Consequently, species-specific heat responses, key regulatory factors, and tipping points of urban tree transpiration remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) multispectral, thermal infrared, and LiDAR observations with field surveys of 665 trees across 20 species to estimate crown-scale transpiration for nearly 50,000 trees. The UAV-based single-source energy balance model captured diurnal evapotranspiration (ET) dynamics and agreed well with eddy covariance measurements (R 2 = 0.86, RMSE = 0.04 mm h −1 ). At the individual-tree scale, UAV-derived crown-scale transpiration agreed closely with sap-flow-derived transpiration (R 2 = 0.88, RMSE = 0.05 mm h −1 ) and leaf area index (LAI)-upscaled portable-photosynthesis-system transpiration estimates (R 2 = 0.88, RMSE = 0.06 mm h −1 ). Compared with the normal day, landscape ET was higher on the extreme-heat day, mainly reflecting higher tree transpiration (0.47 vs. 0.40 mm h −1 ), whereas grassland and shrub ET remained relatively stable. At the species level, three event-specific response groups were identified: enhanced with significantly higher transpiration under extreme heat (12 species), neutral with no significant change (3 species), and suppressed with significantly reduced transpiration (5 species). Random forest analysis identified the temperature vegetation dryness index (TVDI) and leaf-to-air vapor pressure deficit (VPD L ) as dominant controls of crown-scale transpiration, with tree height (TH) also exerting a strong influence. SHAP-derived tipping points for TH were identified at 7.01, 4.42, and 3.65 m in the enhanced, neutral, and suppressed response groups, respectively. SHAP-derived tipping points for TVDI (0.23–0.34) and VPD L (5.34–5.84 kPa) suggested the transition toward soil-water limitation and atmospheric-demand regulation. Overall, this framework enables spatially explicit assessment of urban tree water use and provides a basis for species selection and irrigation management during extreme heat.

title: DynamicVis: Dynamic visual perception for efficient remote sensing foundation models
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: The continuous advancement of remote sensing technology has enabled high-resolution Earth observation; however, interpreting these expansive images using modern Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) remains a significant challenge. Unlike object-centric natural images, remote sensing imagery is fundamentally characterized by extreme target sparsity and massive spatial redundancy. Key objects of interest (e.g., ships, vehicles, scattered buildings) often occupy less than 1% of the spatial extent, surrounded by vast, target-free backgrounds. Many existing VFMs rely on uniform dense processing (e.g., Vision Transformers), while a substantial branch adopts pixel-reconstruction pre-training paradigms (e.g., Masked Autoencoders). These designs may waste substantial computational capacity on modeling redundant backgrounds and dilute the feature representations of small, sparse targets. To bridge this structural misalignment, we propose DynamicVis , a remote sensing visual foundation model explicitly tailored to spatial sparsity in high-resolution imagery, with a focus on large-scale visual pre-training and transferable spatial representations for diverse downstream perception tasks. Architecturally, DynamicVis introduces a Dynamic Region-Aware State Space Model (SSM) that bypasses uniform computation. It adaptively routes and incrementally models only task-relevant, high-salience tokens while employing a parameter-free integration for background context, drastically reducing the complexity of processing ultra-long 2D token sequences ( ∼ 100,000). Crucially, to equip the network with robust spatial-selection capabilities, we propose a novel weakly supervised Region-Level Meta-Embedding Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) pre-training paradigm. Trained on a million-scale dataset, this paradigm promotes foreground-aware regional discrimination in the latent semantic space, mitigating the semantic ambiguity of conventional pixel-reconstruction methods. Extensive evaluations across nine diverse downstream visual perception tasks reveal that DynamicVis achieves competitive performance across region-, instance-, and pixel-level remote sensing tasks, with particularly strong results in sparse-target and instance-level perception tasks (e.g., small object detection and instance segmentation). Notably, DynamicVis processes high-resolution imagery (2048 × 2048) with merely 97 ms latency and 833 MB of memory consumption without employing any acceleration techniques (approximately 6% and 3% of a base ViT, respectively), offering a favorable trade-off between computational scalability and representation accuracy for multi-granular remote sensing analysis. Source code is available at https://github.com/KyanChen/DynamicVis .
